title: Directions Challenge
goal: Your kid writes step-by-step directions for a route or a task, then reads them to you while you follow them exactly, word for word. No pointing, no gestures, no showing. When you end up in the wrong place, your kid works out which words caused it, fixes them, and tries again. It's often hilarious, and it shows kids how hard it is to be truly clear, and how to fix it when they're not.
create: A set of written directions for a route or a task
A fixed version someone can follow without help
A real sense of what makes instructions easy (or hard) to follow
need: A willing follower: you, a sibling, or a friend
A route to walk (around the house, the garden, the park) or a task to complete (a block tower, a sandwich, or a hidden drawing your kid guides you to copy)
Paper and pencil for writing the directions
Optional: a blindfold for an extra challenge

academics.subject: Writing
academics.text: step-by-step instructions, precise words (left, right, numbers, landmarks), and revising for a reader

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: counting and estimating distance, left and right, and quarter turns

academics.subject: Speaking & listening
academics.text: reading instructions aloud and noticing exactly where a listener gets lost

academics.subject: Thinking
academics.text: tracing a problem back to its cause and testing the fix

howTo.intro: The hardest part is playing dumb. You'll know exactly what they mean, and you follow only what they said anyway. Each wrong turn points straight at the words that need fixing, and it's usually where the laughing starts too.

tips.title: Follow word for word
tips.text: If your kid says 'go forward,' keep walking until they say stop. If they say 'turn,' pick a direction yourself. Don't fill in what they meant. The gap between what they said and what they meant is the lesson.

tips.title: Let them find the mistake
tips.text: When you end up in the wrong place, don't explain what went wrong. Just stop and wait. Give your kid the chance to look at their words and work it out.

troubleshoot.q: Your kid doesn't like writing yet
troubleshoot.a: They say each step out loud and you write it down for them.

troubleshoot.q: They get frustrated when it goes wrong
troubleshoot.a: Swap roles for one round, so you're the one giving confusing directions.
Add the blindfold for table tasks like drawing or blocks. On a route, walk right beside the follower, never near stairs.

troubleshoot.q: They say you're going wrong on purpose
troubleshoot.a: Agree up front: when a step could mean two things, you say both and pick one. 'Turn could be left or right. I'm picking right.'

plan.what: Write, run and find what broke (Steps 1 to 3).
Fix it and run it again (Step 4).

skills.name: Clarity
skills.text: saying exactly what you mean, so nobody has to guess

skills.name: Sequencing
skills.text: putting steps in an order someone can follow

skills.name: Perspective-taking
skills.text: realising that what's obvious to you isn't obvious to someone else

skills.name: Problem-solving
skills.text: finding why something didn't work and fixing it

steps.title: Plan it and write it
steps.why: Your kid picks a challenge and writes the first set of directions.
steps.kid: Your kid chooses something to give directions for: a route (kitchen to mailbox) or a task (a block tower, a sandwich, or a hidden drawing they make and keep secret). Then they write the directions one step per line, saying exactly how far or how many: 'take 4 steps,' not 'go a bit.'
steps.you: Help brainstorm a few ideas from the list below, then let your kid choose. Agree on the rule together: words only, no pointing or showing. While they write, don't look. You'll find out how clear the directions are in Step 2.
starters: Hidden drawing: a house with one window
ask: What's something you know how to do that would be hard to explain?
If you write 'turn,' how will I know which way?
steps.tip: Pick something your kid knows well but has never had to explain out loud. Knowing how to do something and explaining it are very different skills.

levels.explore: Draw each step as a picture card (a foot with a number, an arrow, a door), up to 5 cards, and say each one out loud.
levels.develop: Aim for 6 to 10 steps, using distances (12 steps) or landmarks (the big chair).
levels.extend: Add a checkpoint every few steps, like 'You should now see the front door.'

steps.title: Give the directions
steps.why: The first test run. You follow the directions exactly, and both of you see what happens.
steps.kid: Your kid reads the directions out loud, one step at a time, and waits while you do each one. Words only. If you go the wrong way, they don't correct you yet. They just watch and make a small mark next to the step where it happened.
steps.you: Do exactly what you hear, nothing more. If a direction is unclear, make your best guess and do that, even if you're pretty sure it's not what your kid meant. No questions on this first try. For the hidden drawing, reveal both drawings side by side at the end.
ask: At which step did things start to go wrong?
Did I do what you said, or what you meant?
steps.tip: This first run is supposed to go a bit wrong. That's not failure. It's exactly what Step 3 needs.

levels.explore: Read your directions and watch. Afterward, point to where things went off track.
levels.develop: Give no hints at all, and mark every step where something unexpected happened.
levels.extend: After each step, quietly write what you expected and what actually happened.

steps.title: Find the breakdowns
steps.why: Together, you work out why each step went wrong.
steps.kid: Your kid goes back through the directions with you, line by line. For each step that went wrong, they figure out why: was it too vague, was a step missing, were the steps in the wrong order, or did they assume you knew something you didn't?
steps.you: Now you can talk. At each confusing step, say what went through your head: 'When you said turn, I didn't know which way.' Keep it about the words, never about your kid. Let them name the cause before you suggest one.
ask: What did you assume I would know that I didn't?
Was the problem what you said, or what you didn't say?
steps.tip: The big lesson here: when someone gets lost, the problem usually isn't the listener. It's the message.

levels.explore: Circle the steps that didn't work, and say what went wrong in your own words.
levels.develop: Next to each circled step, write the cause: vague, missing step, wrong order, or assumed.
levels.extend: Make a table: what you said, what I did, and why. Look for the mistake you made most.

steps.title: Fix it and run it again
steps.why: Your kid rewrites what broke, and you test the new version.
steps.kid: Your kid rewrites only the steps they marked, adding what was missing: how far, which way, a landmark, an exact number. Then they read the new version to you from the start, the same way as Step 2, or try it on someone new.
steps.you: Don't rewrite it for them. If they're stuck, ask a question instead: 'How will I know when to stop?' Then follow the new version just as literally as before, and compare it with the first run together.
ask: Could anyone get this new version wrong?
Was the second run better? Where exactly?
steps.tip: When the second run works, say so out loud: 'I didn't have to guess once that time.' That moment is the payoff.

levels.explore: Fix the 2 or 3 steps that caused the most trouble, then try again.
levels.develop: Rewrite every step that went wrong, and compare the second run with the first.
levels.extend: '6 big steps' depends on whose legs. Test one step with a short and a tall follower, then add a landmark so it works for both.

steps.title: Write it for a real visitor
steps.why: Directions for someone who actually needs them are the real test.
steps.kid: Your kid writes new directions for someone who really needs them: a guest finding the bathroom, a friend walking from the corner, a babysitter finding the first-aid kit. They use every fix from the first set, leave the directions out, then ask how it went and fix any step that failed.
steps.you: Pick a real reason together, then stay out of the writing. If you can see a step will fail, ask 'What will they see right there?' and let your kid decide.
ask: Where did the visitor slow down or ask?
What will you write differently next time?
steps.tip: End by picking the next challenge together: a route if you did a task, or a task if you did a route.

levels.explore: Draw picture-card directions from the front door to the bathroom, and tape them up for a visitor.
levels.develop: Write directions for a real guest, leave them out, and fix every step they asked about.
levels.extend: Write the same route twice, for someone walking and someone on a bike. Which steps had to change, and why?

conclusion.headline: They can find the exact words that sent you the wrong way.
conclusion.text: Ask them for directions to something in the house, no pointing. Listen for numbers, left and right, and landmarks like 'past the big chair'. If they pause to picture what you'd see from where you stand, they're thinking like the listener now.
conclusion.celebrate: On the second run, the moment you land exactly where they meant, say it: 'Same route, new words, and I didn't go wrong once. You fixed that.'
extensions: Give directions over the phone to someone at the park, who can't see you at all
Write directions with no numbers allowed, only landmarks, then a set with no landmarks, only numbers. Which one got the follower there?
Write directions to a hidden treat and leave them for someone to find
Race the clock: can your partner finish in under 3 minutes using only your directions?

signs: 'Left' and 'right' start turning up whenever they explain something
Ask where something is and you get a number or a landmark back
When someone misunderstands, they check their own words first
makeItReal: When you're out walking, let your kid give the directions home, words only, and follow them exactly, wrong turns and all.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.caption: From our house: one stove, drawn twice. Every difference is a word that wasn't clear yet.

done.text: Done? Tap it on your trail so it shows up in your kid's record.
done.label: Open my trail

onTheRoad: Write directions from where you're staying to the nearest bakery or shop, then follow them together, word for word.
Ask a local for directions, with your help, and notice whether they use landmarks, street names or just point.
Learn the local words for left, right, straight and stop, and guide a family member using only those words.
backHome: Rewrite one set of directions at home in the landmark style you heard on the road, and test it on someone.

lesson.text: Clear directions answer three questions at every step: how far, which way, and to what. Leave one out and the follower has to guess.
lesson.before: 'Go to the kitchen. Turn. Open it.'

model.line: Walk 6 big steps to the kitchen door.
Turn left so the fridge is in front of you.

lesson.modelNote: 'Open it' made sense to the writer, who could see the fridge. The fix names the distance, the turn and the thing, so nobody has to guess.

classroom.intro: This one is made for pairs: one writes directions, the other follows them word for word. A classroom full of desks, doors and chairs gives every pair a route, and the wrong turns are just as funny.

tips.d: One student reads the directions while the partner follows exactly, then they swap. Each pair needs only paper, a pencil and a route or task they chose.
Use routes like desk to pencil sharpener, door to the reading corner, or classroom to the office. Keep any hallway routes supervised and within your sight.
When space is tight, use the task versions: a 4-block tower, a paper plane, or a hidden drawing the partner copies from spoken directions only, sitting back to back.
Before pairs start, follow one student's directions at the front, walking forward until told to stop. The class sees why 'turn' needs a direction and 'forward' needs a distance.
Post Step 3's four causes on the board: vague, missing step, wrong order, assumed. Explore kids circle steps, Develop kids label each cause, and Extend kids build the said, did, why table.
Pairs write directions someone really needs, like the front door to your classroom or to the school library. Tape them up for a guest or substitute and collect their comments.

classroom.timing: Two sessions of 40 to 45 minutes work well: writing, the first run and finding breakdowns in the first, then fixing and rerunning in the second. Step 5's visitor directions can run over the following week.
